payload.name: Extract Explicit Plans and Intentions
payload.description: Use when a speaker states what they plan to do, intend, or want to do regarding an event, project, or upcoming occasion.
content: During extraction, treat explicit first-person statements of intention (e.g., 'I want to...', 'I plan to...', 'I'm going to...') as memory-worthy and create a plan memory for the speaker when the statement expresses what they intend to do.

If a plan is tied to an already-extracted event or project candidate, either include the stated plan in that event memory or create a separate plan candidate; do not drop the plan while summarizing the event.
Stop after capturing the stated plan and its target event; do not infer additional plans or expand the scope.

candidates.solves: When a speaker explicitly states a plan or intention for an upcoming event or project, extraction sometimes records only the event overview and omits the stated plan, making it impossible to answer future questions about what the speaker intends to do. This Skill ensures explicit first-person plans are captured as plan memories or included in the related event memory.

payload.name: Extract Job Start Events from Casual Mentions
payload.description: When a speaker mentions starting a new job, position, or role, even in small talk, during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat any explicit statement that the speaker started a new job, position, or role as an event candidate, even if it appears in casual conversation or as an aside.
Include the job title or role and any stated start time; resolve relative time like 'last week' against the message timestamp to compute the actual date.
Record the speaker as the subject and use memory kind 'event'; do not fold the job start into a pet, project, or preference candidate.
Stop after capturing the stated job change; do not infer employer, salary, or other details unless explicitly mentioned.

candidates.solves: Construction pipelines often ignore explicit life changes such as starting a new job when they appear in casual small talk, so later questions about when the person began the role cannot be answered. This skill ensures job/role start statements are extracted as dated event memories.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Collaboration Agreements
payload.description: When two participants explicitly agree or decide to collaborate on a shared activity or content, extract it as a memory candidate, even if the agreement is stated enthusiastically or in casual wording.
content: During extraction, treat an explicit mutual agreement to collaborate on a shared activity (e.g., creating content, working on a project, managing accounts) as a durable event or relationship memory candidate.
Capture the collaborators, the agreed activity, and the date/time of the agreement from the message or session timestamp.
When the agreement is confirmed in a later message after earlier offers or interest, the final confirming message is sufficient evidence; create one candidate for the decision.
Stop after capturing the agreement; do not infer outcomes, add unspoken tasks, or create separate memories for every enthusiastic reply.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes fail to persist explicit agreements to collaborate when they are expressed in casual or enthusiastic language at the end of a multi-turn discussion, even though earlier offers and advice were captured. This Skill ensures mutual collaboration decisions are extracted as event or relationship memories with the parties, the agreed activity, and the timestamp.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Motivational Drivers
payload.description: Use when a speaker explicitly states what motivates or drives them or their group to improve, persist, or succeed.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly names what motivates or drives them or their group to improve, persist, or succeed, create a state or preference candidate capturing the driver and the subject, even if the message is small talk or contains no direct question.
Do not require the motivation to be tied to a named project; capture the stated reason from everyday narrative and resolve relative time from the session timestamp.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated driver; do not infer additional unstated motivations or add unrelated details.

candidates.solves: Extraction misses explicit statements that name what motivates or drives a speaker or their group to improve, persist, or succeed, because these statements are often brief, occur in casual conversation, and are not tied to a named project or question.

payload.name: Extract Discovered Places as Event Memories
payload.description: When a speaker reports finding, discovering, checking out, or stumbling upon a place (park, open space, cafe, spot), during extraction or when updating a plan memory.
content: During extraction, when a message states that the speaker or the speaker and others found, discovered, checked out, or stumbled upon a place, create a separate event memory capturing who, what place, and when; do not store it only as a plan or intention.
If a later message reports visiting that discovered place, update or keep that event memory instead of folding the visit into a plan memory.
During CRUD, when updating a plan memory, preserve any earlier discovered/visited place facts as distinct event memories; do not overwrite them with new plans or object_text changes.
Stop after capturing the discovered place once; do not add duplicate memories for later casual mentions.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes record only a future plan (e.g., intending to hike) and fail to store an already-completed discovery or visit of a place, so later updates to the plan lose the fact that the place was checked out. This skill ensures discovered/visited places are stored as separate event memories and preserved during plan updates.

payload.name: Preserve All Stated Intentions in Event Plans
payload.description: When extracting an event or plan where the speaker explicitly states multiple intentions or reasons, include every stated reason in the memory candidate.
content: During extraction, if a message states why the speaker plans to attend or do something, capture every explicitly stated intention or reason in the event/plan candidate.
Scan the source message for all purpose clauses (e.g., 'to ...', 'because ...', 'so that ...') and list each one; do not paraphrase away or merge distinct reasons.
Stop after all stated reasons are included; do not add unmentioned motives.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes paraphrase a memory candidate and drop one of several explicitly stated reasons or intentions behind a plan or event, causing later questions about the person's motivation to fail. This skill ensures every explicitly stated purpose is preserved in the extracted event or plan memory.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Stated Preferences
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states what they enjoy, like, or prefer (e.g., types of films, books, activities), even in a turn that also mentions a project or plan.
content: During extraction, create a preference memory whenever a speaker explicitly states something they enjoy or like, even if the same turn includes a project, plan, or other event.
Do not let a project-focused extraction replace or suppress the explicit preference; each explicitly stated preference should be its own candidate.
Extract only the categories or items explicitly named as enjoyed, and stop after capturing the stated likes; do not infer additional genres or preferences.

candidates.solves: Conversations often mix several facts in one turn. When a user explicitly states a preference (such as enjoying a type of film) alongside a project, plan, or other event, the construction agent may capture only the project and drop the preference, causing a missing memory for later questions. This skill ensures explicit preference statements are extracted independently.

payload.name: Extract Brief Planned Gatherings and Events
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly mentions organizing, hosting, or planning an event or gathering, even briefly in small talk, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly says they are organizing, hosting, or planning an event or gathering (e.g., party, meetup, tournament, get-together), create an event candidate capturing the event, the organizer, and any explicit time reference, even when the mention is brief or embedded in a reply about someone else's plans.

Resolve relative time references (e.g., 'this weekend', 'two weekends later') using the message/session timestamp to an absolute date or at least the month, so future temporal questions can be answered.
Create one candidate per announced event and stop once the organizer, event, and time are captured; do not infer guests, location, or other details that are not explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: Construction misses explicit planned events or gatherings announced in small talk, especially when the speaker is replying to another person's plans. The system should extract the event, organizer, and a resolved time reference even from a brief sentence so future questions about what someone is organizing can be answered.

payload.name: Extract New Activity Intentions and Tryouts
payload.description: Use during extraction when a speaker expresses interest in, plans to try, or states they are trying a new hobby or activity, including in reply to a suggestion.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly says they are considering, planning, or starting a new hobby or activity, create a candidate memory for that activity with any stated timeframe.
Use memory kind 'event' when the speaker states they will try or are trying it; otherwise use 'preference' or 'state' for interest alone.
Do not skip such statements because they are replies, small talk, or acknowledgments; treat the speaker's own stated intention as sufficient evidence.
Capture only the activity and facts explicitly stated; do not infer acceptance of an unmentioned suggestion, and stop once the activity is captured.
During CRUD, if a matching memory for the same activity already exists, MERGE or UPDATE it instead of creating a duplicate.

candidates.solves: The construction agent sometimes fails to extract a speaker's own adoption of a new hobby or activity when it appears in casual replies to suggestions, treating the message as small talk or as belonging only to the other speaker's offer. This skill ensures explicit intentions to try or take up an activity become durable memories.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Business or Venture Status
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states the current condition of their business, store, or venture, extract it as a state memory.
content: During extraction, when a speaker reports the current status of a business, store, or venture they own or run (e.g., 'doing great', 'struggling'), create a state memory with subject=speaker, the named entity, and the stated status.
Set world_start to the message/session date and use only explicit wording; do not infer status from enthusiasm, obstacles, or future plans.
Stop after capturing the stated status; do not add unrelated details from the same message unless they are separate explicit facts.

candidates.solves: During memory extraction, explicit statements about the current condition of a person's business, store, or venture are often skipped because existing skills focus on projects, events, and emotional support. This Skill ensures these direct status assertions are captured as durable state memories so future questions about the business can be answered.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Motivations for Ongoing Improvement
payload.description: When a user explicitly states what motivates or inspires them to keep improving at an activity, even as a reflective aside without a question, project, or event.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states a love, passion, or reason that motivates them to keep improving at an activity, create a preference or state memory capturing both the activity and the stated motivator; do not skip the turn because the statement is reflective, contains no question, or is not attached to a project or event.
Keep the stated motivator as its own facet in the memory rather than merging it into a vague preference summary or inferring additional unstated reasons.
Stop after capturing the explicitly stated motivator and its immediate activity; do not broaden to other activities or projects from the same session.

candidates.solves: Construction agents often omit explicit motivational statements when they appear in reflective conversation rather than as a project, goal, or event. This Skill ensures that a user's stated love, passion, or reason for improving is captured as a preference or state memory.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Events on Update
payload.description: When a new message describes an event or fact that differs from an existing memory (different date, milestone, or topic), before applying an UPDATE verify whether the existing memory is truly the same fact; otherwise ADD a separate memory.
content: During the CRUD/update stage, before applying UPDATE to an existing memory, check whether the new message describes the same event/fact as the existing memory (same subject, same event type, and same time period).
If the new message describes a distinct event, even with the same people, do not overwrite the existing memory; create a new ADD candidate for the new event.
Preserve the original memory's content, world_start, and facts unless the new message explicitly corrects or supersedes that same fact.

When two related but different events exist (e.g., a pregnancy announcement and a later marriage announcement), keep them as separate memories and only update one when the new evidence directly revises that same memory.

candidates.solves: Prevents a later message about a different event from overwriting an earlier distinct memory during construction updates. When a new message involves the same people but describes a separate milestone, date, or topic, the agent should ADD a new memory instead of UPDATE-ing the old one, preserving previously stored facts.

payload.name: Preserve Prior Facts on Memory Update
payload.description: When updating an existing memory about a project or activity, if the new message adds details or mentions a related topic without explicitly contradicting the stored facts, preserve the original facts instead of overwriting them.
content: During UPDATE on an existing memory, first compare the new message's claims with the memory's current explicit facts.

If the new message only adds detail, reframes the topic, or mentions a related project, do not replace the existing memory; instead add a new candidate or merge only the genuinely new attributes while keeping the original facts unchanged.

Only overwrite a stored fact when the new message explicitly contradicts it. When it does, preserve the old factual span by setting world_end or retaining the older version, and do not move world_start unless the message explicitly corrects the start date.
Stop after deciding the update; do not search for additional evidence or expand the memory beyond what the message states.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes replaces a previously stored, still-valid fact (e.g., a project name or start date) when a later message describes a related but different aspect of the same activity. This destroys evidence needed for temporal queries. This skill prevents destructive overwrites by requiring an explicit contradiction before replacing facts, and by keeping old facts or creating separate memories when the new message merely adds or shifts topic.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Event Memories on Update
payload.description: When a later message describes a different event than an existing memory, during CRUD, do not overwrite the existing event; add a separate memory and preserve prior facts.
content: During CRUD, before UPDATEing an event memory, check whether the incoming fact is the same event (same activity and time) as the stored memory. If it is a different event, do not overwrite; ADD a new event memory.
When the incoming message enriches the same event, UPDATE or MERGE may be used, but preserve any previously stored distinct facts that remain true.
Never reuse a memory ID for an unrelated event just because the subject, companion, or memory kind matches; each distinct activity/event needs its own memory.
Stop once the new event is stored; do not add duplicate memories for repeated mentions of the same event.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of previously stored event facts when a later message describes a different activity for the same person or companion. The agent may incorrectly UPDATE an existing event memory in place, replacing its activity and date with the new event instead of creating a separate memory.

payload.name: Verify Redundancy Before Skipping Candidate
payload.description: Use during CRUD/decision when a candidate is about to be SKIPped as already covered or updated; verify the referenced memory actually exists before skipping.
content: During CRUD/decision stage, before marking any candidate as SKIP for redundancy, verify that a memory containing the same facts actually exists in the retrieved existing-memory pool or was accepted earlier in the current batch.
If the skip reason references an 'updated memory' that cannot be found in the pool or in accepted updates, do not skip; instead ADD or UPDATE to persist the candidate.
Only skip when the identical information is verifiably present in the relevant memory records; when in doubt, keep the candidate to avoid information loss.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of extracted facts when the Construction Agent skips a candidate believing the information already exists in an updated memory, but no such memory is actually present in the current pool or batch. Instills a verification step before SKIP decisions to ensure redundancy claims are grounded in real memory records.

payload.name: Preserve Existing Facts in Memory Merge
payload.description: During CRUD, when merging or updating an existing memory with new evidence, use this guidance to prevent older facts from being overwritten.
content: During CRUD, before applying a MERGE or UPDATE to an existing memory, read the current version's content and list every concrete fact it stores (activities, preferences, events, relationships).
Apply the change as a superset: keep all those existing facts in the new version, adding or replacing only content the new evidence explicitly changes or contradicts.
If the new evidence concerns a different topic with no explicit contradiction, create a separate memory for it and leave the existing memory unchanged instead of merging unrelated content.
After writing the new version, verify that every previously stored concrete fact is still present; restore any that were dropped.
Stop once old facts are preserved and new evidence is incorporated; do not add unrelated inferences or extra memories.

candidates.solves: Memory construction loses previously stored facts when a later MERGE or UPDATE replaces an existing memory's content with new evidence instead of combining them. This skill ensures CRUD operations preserve the old memory's concrete facts while adding new evidence, and avoid merging unrelated topics into one memory.

payload.name: Keep Specific Events Not Covered by General Memories
payload.description: When deciding whether to ADD or SKIP an event candidate and the only existing memory is a broader general statement, ADD the event instead of skipping it as already represented.
content: During CRUD decisions, compare an event candidate against existing memories for the same concrete occurrence: same subject, action, object, time, and emotional reaction.

If the existing memory states only a general trait, preference, or impact and does not already contain the specific event details, do not SKIP as already represented; ADD or MERGE the event candidate.
Preserve the distinct event even when it illustrates a broader theme, because later questions may ask about the specific episode or feeling.
Stop after one event per occurrence; do not add multiple paraphrases of the same event.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of specific episodic facts during memory construction when a candidate is incorrectly skipped because a general memory about the same person or topic already exists. It preserves concrete events and feelings that may be asked about later.

payload.name: Verify Existing Memory Before SKIP
payload.description: When a construction CRUD decision is about to SKIP a candidate because it claims the information is already covered by an existing memory, use this skill.
content: During CRUD, before SKIPping a candidate as duplicate or already covered, confirm the covering memory is present in the current retrieved memory pool and explicitly contains the same fact.
If no matching memory exists, ADD the candidate; do not infer coverage from earlier sessions or from a general sense that the topic was discussed.
Only UPDATE or MERGE when the existing memory is verified; if the pool lacks the memory, adding preserves the new evidence.

candidates.solves: Prevents construction decisions from skipping newly extracted evidence by assuming it is already stored. A candidate is dropped as a duplicate even though no matching memory exists in the retrieved pool, so the fact is never persisted and later questions cannot be answered.

payload.name: Merge New Category Members into Existing Memory Instead of Replacing
payload.description: When a user reveals an additional item in a category already stored or likely to be stored (e.g., allergies, dietary restrictions, dislikes), during extraction or update.
content: During extraction, if a user explicitly states a restriction or attribute in a recurring category (e.g., allergies, dietary limits, dislikes), create a candidate for that fact even when it appears in casual conversation; do not wait for a direct question.

During CRUD, when a new candidate adds another member of a category already present in an existing memory (e.g., another allergy on a memory that lists allergies), do not replace the existing content with only the new member. Preserve previously stored members and append the new one in the same memory or merge into it.

Use a correction/overwrite only when the new statement explicitly contradicts or supersedes an earlier fact; for additive facts, keep prior content and record the new item with its own evidence and date.
After merging, stop; do not expand into exhaustive searches or add unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of previously stored facts when a later message adds another member of the same category (e.g., an additional allergy or dietary restriction). The agent replaced the whole memory with only the new item and also skipped extracting the first mention of a related restriction, so later answers missed earlier facts.

payload.name: Preserve prior specifics when enriching memories
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory, use this if the new content is more general, emotional, or abstract than the stored fact, or if the update would drop previously captured details.
content: During CRUD, before updating or merging an existing memory, compare the new content against the stored facts. Preserve every specific, time-bound fact already captured (e.g., doctor visits, diagnoses, dates, locations) unless directly contradicted by new evidence.

If new messages add broader context such as general struggles, feelings, or quotes about the same topic, do not replace the concrete earlier fact with that framing. Create an enriched version that keeps the old specifics and appends the new nuance.

If an update would remove a previously captured fact that is not contradicted, treat the update as a loss: retain the old detail and add the new information instead. Stop once the memory contains both the preserved facts and the relevant new context; do not expand into unrelated details.

candidates.solves: During CRUD, an existing memory that contains a concrete, time-bound fact is sometimes overwritten by a later, more general summary that drops the fact, making it impossible to answer future questions about the specific event. This Skill ensures updates preserve previously stored specifics while incorporating new context.

payload.name: Preserve Prior Facts When Updating Memory
payload.description: Apply during CRUD when a new message adds a detail to an existing preference, state, or profile memory, to avoid replacing older supported facts with a narrower statement.
content: During CRUD, before UPDATE or MERGE, compare the new evidence with the stored content. If the new fact is additional rather than contradictory, preserve the old facts and append the new detail instead of overwriting the whole memory.
Use MERGE or an additive UPDATE when the prior facts are still supported by earlier messages; do not rewrite the memory to only the new detail.
Do not mark the memory as a correction or change its kind/start date unless the source message explicitly states the previous fact was wrong or no longer true.

candidates.solves: When later information adds a new detail to an existing memory, the Construction Agent sometimes overwrites the entire memory with the new detail, losing previously supported facts. This skill prevents that by requiring the agent to preserve old facts unless the new evidence explicitly contradicts them.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Events During Memory Update
payload.description: When updating or merging an event memory with new evidence that describes a different occurrence of the same activity, use this to keep both events separate.
content: During UPDATE or MERGE of an event memory, compare the new evidence's time and ordinal (e.g., 'first', 'regional', 'fourth') with the existing memory. If they describe distinct occurrences, do not overwrite the existing content; keep the original event and add a separate event memory for the new one.

Only update/replace the existing memory when the new evidence clearly refers to the same occurrence. If times or ordinals differ, preserve the original event's who/what/date and record the new event with its own date.
Stop once the original event and the new event are each represented in a memory; do not add unrelated details.

candidates.solves: Prevents losing an earlier event when new evidence describes a different occurrence of the same activity; an UPDATE or MERGE must not overwrite a distinct past event with a newer one.

payload.name: Preserve Prior Facts on Memory Update
payload.description: During CRUD, when updating an existing memory with new or more detailed information, merge new facts while preserving prior facts and dates that remain true.
content: During CRUD, when new information updates an existing memory, do not replace the whole content with a new summary; merge the new facts into the previous content and keep every prior fact that is still true and not contradicted.
Preserve the existing world_start (begin date) unless the new message explicitly revises it; do not reset it to the timestamp of the later message.
If the prior memory records a duration or implied start date derived from an earlier statement, carry that date into the updated version rather than dropping it.
If the new message contradicts one field, keep the newer value, but retain the other previously recorded facts that remain valid.

candidates.solves: Construction agents frequently lose already-recorded facts when a later message updates an existing memory: the whole memory is replaced and time fields are reset, erasing earlier details such as names, counts, or the implied adoption/start year. This skill ensures UPDATE operations merge new information with the prior memory and preserve facts and world_start dates that remain true.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Prior Plans on Update
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with a new plan or event, use if the new evidence involves a different activity, date, or companion than the stored memory.
content: During CRUD, before UPDATE or MERGE of an existing memory, compare the new plan's activity, participants, and timing with the stored memory's existing facets.

If the new plan is a different activity or a separate scheduled occurrence (e.g., painting next Saturday vs. kayaking on a later date), do not overwrite the existing memory content; create a new memory for the new plan or merge only the new distinct facets while preserving the old plan and its date.
Treat evidence as contradictory only when it explicitly denies or replaces the exact same planned activity and time; otherwise preserve the prior fact.
Stop after storing the new plan once; do not create near-duplicate memories of the same plan.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes overwrite a previously stored plan or event memory when a later, unrelated plan is mentioned, discarding the original fact. This skill ensures distinct plans with different activities, dates, or participants are kept as separate memories, and prior facts are preserved unless new evidence directly contradicts them.

payload.name: Preserve Existing Facts When Enriching Memories
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with new details during CRUD, or when building an enrichment candidate during extraction.
content: During CRUD, when an UPDATE or MERGE has update_type 'enrichment', retain all existing explicit facts already stored in the memory (names, counts, dates, locations, etc.) unless the new message directly contradicts them.
Combine the new details with the old content instead of replacing it; only drop a previously stored fact when the latest message explicitly says it changed or was wrong.

During extraction, when drafting a candidate that targets an existing memory, include the existing memory's durable facts along with the newly stated attributes, so the subsequent CRUD update does not lose them.

candidates.solves: Prevents memory updates from silently dropping previously captured facts when new related details are added. For example, when a later message adds breed information about a person's pets, the update should preserve the already-stored pet names rather than replacing them with only the new attributes.

payload.name: Preserve Prior Facts When Enriching Memories
payload.description: Use when updating or merging an existing memory with new messages that add details about the same subject, to ensure previously stored explicit facts are retained.
content: During CRUD (UPDATE/MERGE), compare any proposed new memory content against the existing version it targets before writing.

Retain every explicit fact already stored in the existing memory unless a new message directly contradicts it; add newly stated details as additional facets rather than replacing the old content with a narrower paraphrase.
Stop after consolidating the preserved facts with the new explicit details; do not infer or add unrelated attributes.

candidates.solves: When the Construction Agent enriches an existing memory with new conversation details, it sometimes rewrites the memory as a narrower summary and drops explicit facts stored earlier, making those facts unavailable for later questions. This skill ensures that UPDATE and MERGE operations preserve prior explicit attributes while adding new ones.

payload.name: Verify Event Coverage Before SKIP
payload.description: Use during CRUD decisions before skipping an event candidate as already represented; check whether the existing memory covers the specific event details, not just a related theme.
content: During CRUD, before SKIPping a candidate as already represented, compare against the matched memory's specific facts: subject, action, object, and time. A general trait, impact, or preference statement does not cover a specific event.

If the existing memory only overlaps thematically (e.g., a writing-impact profile vs. a received-letter event), do not SKIP; ADD a new event memory or MERGE only if the event details are already present.
Check the full existing memory content for the event's distinguishing facts; do not assume an enrichment update will later add them, because it may not.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions sometimes skip a correctly extracted event because a related profile or preference memory seems to cover the same theme, losing the specific event and its timing. This guides CRUD to require event-specific facts before skipping.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Event Facts on Update
payload.description: When updating an existing event memory with new message content, first check whether the new activity/event is the same as the memory's; if it is a distinct past event, keep the original memory and ADD a new one.
content: During CRUD/update, before replacing an existing memory's content or world_start with new event details, verify that the new message describes the same event (same activity, companions, and timeframe).
If the new event differs in activity, companions, or time, do not UPDATE the existing memory; instead ADD a new memory for the new event and leave the original unchanged.
When uncertain, prefer adding a distinct memory over overwriting; multiple past events with the same subject at different times must coexist.

candidates.solves: Prevents construction updates from overwriting an earlier event memory when a later message mentions a different event. The agent should distinguish same-event updates from distinct events and preserve original facts by adding a separate memory.

payload.name: Detail-Level Coverage Check Before Skip
payload.description: When deciding whether to SKIP or MERGE a candidate during construction, check whether the existing memory explicitly contains every distinct fact in the candidate; apply before any SKIP or MERGE.
content: During CRUD decisions, before SKIPping or MERGEing a candidate, verify the target memory explicitly contains every distinct factual detail in the candidate (who, what, when, and any specific artifact or event).
If any detail is missing, do not SKIP or MERGE; add the candidate as a new memory or enrich the existing memory with the missing details.
Do not treat a broader thematic statement (e.g., 'writing brought comfort to others') as covering a specific distinct fact (e.g., 'someone wrote her a letter about her blog post on a hard moment').
Stop after preserving the missing details; do not rewrite or duplicate unrelated existing content.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes discard a correctly extracted event candidate because an existing memory covers the same subject or a related outcome, but the existing memory omits a specific factual detail. This skill prevents loss of answerable facts by requiring a detail-level coverage check before SKIP/MERGE decisions.

payload.name: Preserve Existing Facts When Enriching Memories
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing memory with additional details from later messages, apply this to keep previously recorded explicit facts that remain true.
content: During UPDATE or MERGE operations that enrich an existing memory, add or integrate the newly stated details into the current content rather than replacing the whole content.
Before rewriting, list the explicit facts already stored; keep every fact that is still true and not contradicted by the new evidence, including concrete outcomes and achievements.
If new details refine the subject (e.g., project focus), update those specifics but do not delete older explicit accomplishments unless the new source explicitly denies or supersedes them.
Stop once the new details are incorporated; do not add unrelated facts or rephrase away the speaker's concrete wording.

candidates.solves: Memory UPDATE operations that enrich an existing record with new details often overwrite the previous content, dropping earlier explicit facts such as achievements or outcomes. This skill teaches the Construction Agent to preserve all still-true explicitly stated facts when appending or integrating new information, preventing later queries from missing evidence-backed claims.

payload.name: Preserve Distinct Events on Update
payload.description: When updating or merging memories during CRUD, if a new message describes a different event than the existing memory, even for the same person, keep both as separate memories instead of overwriting.
content: During CRUD, before applying UPDATE or MERGE to an existing memory, determine whether the incoming evidence describes the same real-world event or a distinct event. Distinct if the event type, time, or occurrence differs (e.g., pregnancy vs marriage announcement).
If the events are distinct, do not overwrite or replace the existing memory. ADD a separate memory for the new event and retain the old one intact.

Only UPDATE/MERGE when the new information truly corrects or extends the same event (e.g., a more precise date or explicit retraction). Do not assume same subject or near timing implies the same event.
After preserving the distinct event, stop; do not create redundant copies of the same new event.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of previously stored facts when a later message describes a new event related to the same person or partner. Construction agents sometimes overwrite an existing event memory with a different event that shares the same subject or close timing, erasing the original fact.

payload.name: Preserve Existing Explicit Facts During Memory Merge
payload.description: When updating or merging an existing memory with new evidence, use this to retain all explicit claims from the prior version unless directly contradicted.
content: During CRUD-stage UPDATE/MERGE, compare the existing memory's explicit facts with the new evidence before changing content.

Keep every explicit claim from the existing version (including specific passions, stated beliefs, and named effects) unless the new evidence directly contradicts it; express both old and new facts in the merged memory.

Do not reduce a specific claim to a broader category (for example, do not turn 'passion for fantasy stuff' into 'enjoys fantasy genres') and do not let a newly mentioned theme replace the memory's previous focus.

If the new evidence concerns a different domain, preserve the current memory in place and create or update a separate memory for the new domain; change only fields the new evidence actually contradicts.
Preserve the original world_start unless the new evidence explicitly indicates a new start; stop after merging explicit facts and do not infer additional relationships.

candidates.solves: Later messages often introduce a related but different topic, and an update/merge can rewrite a precise memory into a broader summary, dropping exact claims (like a specific passion or its stated effect) that future questions rely on. This skill makes update/merge operations combine new evidence with the existing memory's explicit facts instead of replacing them.

payload.name: Extract Third-Party Assessments Separately
payload.description: When a message contains both an explicit third-party assessment (e.g., doctor's statement, professional opinion) and a person's attitude or emotion, extract the assessment as its own candidate.
content: During extraction, when a speaker reports an explicit factual statement from another person (e.g., a doctor's assessment, diagnosis, or prognosis) while also expressing an attitude or emotion, create a separate memory candidate for the factual statement, preserving the source and exact content.
Do not let a summarizing state memory about the person's attitude (e.g., 'staying positive') replace or absorb the explicit third-party statement.
During CRUD, if an existing memory contains the attitude but omits the stated assessment, update or merge it to include the assessment rather than leaving the incomplete version.
Stop after capturing the assessment and the attitude; do not add inferred medical details, unstated severity, or speculative outcomes.

candidates.solves: Prevents loss of explicit third-party factual statements (e.g., professional assessments, diagnoses, or prognoses) when extraction focuses on a person's attitude or emotional state, by requiring such statements to be captured as separate memory candidates.

payload.name: Preserve All Explicitly Stated Attributes
payload.description: When a user explicitly lists multiple qualities, reasons, or attributes for liking, admiring, or valuing someone or something during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly enumerates multiple qualities, reasons, or attributes (e.g., 'brave, selfless, down-to-earth attitude'), preserve every listed item in the candidate memory; do not paraphrase away or drop any of them.
Record the attributes closely to the speaker's wording and keep them together in one memory when they describe the same target and relationship.
During CRUD, if a matching memory already exists, UPDATE or MERGE it to add any explicitly stated attributes that are missing, then stop; do not infer or add unmentioned attributes.

candidates.solves: When extracting memories from statements where a user explicitly lists multiple qualities, reasons, or attributes (for example, why they admire a person or character), the extraction step sometimes paraphrases the list into a summary and drops some listed items. This causes later questions about the omitted attributes to fail. The skill ensures every explicitly stated attribute is preserved in the memory so the full set of stated reasons remains retrievable.

payload.name: Preserve All Enumerated Categories in Extraction
payload.description: When a message confirms a question and adds multiple distinct people, groups, or items, during extraction preserve each explicitly named category.
content: During extraction, when a speaker enumerates two or more distinct people, groups, items, or attributes in a single message (including affirmations like 'Definitely!' followed by 'and...'), preserve each distinct category explicitly in the candidate content.

Do not merge or paraphrase the enumeration into a subset or shift modifiers between nouns; e.g., 'old friends and teammates from other tournaments' must yield both 'old friends' and 'teammates from other tournaments', not 'old teammates'.
Stop once every explicitly stated category is captured; do not infer unmentioned categories or expand the list.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates sometimes paraphrase enumerated groups and drop an explicitly stated category, so future questions miss a fact. This skill keeps every distinct category named in an enumeration in the memory candidate.

payload.name: Extract all distinct durable facts per message
payload.description: During extraction, when one message contains two or more independent durable facts about a person, create a separate memory candidate for each fact; do not keep only the most prominent or emotionally salient one.
content: During extraction, if a single message states multiple distinct durable facts about the speaker or another person (e.g., receiving a specific item and experiencing a life event), emit each fact as its own candidate memory instead of combining them or keeping only one.

When one fact is emotionally prominent (e.g., a job loss), do not let it suppress other explicitly stated durable facts in the same message; each explicit durable claim remains eligible for extraction.
Stop after capturing each explicitly stated durable fact; do not infer additional facts or expand beyond the message's content.

candidates.solves: During construction extraction, a single message can contain multiple distinct durable facts, but the extractor sometimes captures only the most salient or emotionally prominent one and drops the others. This skill ensures that every explicitly stated durable fact in a message is emitted as its own candidate memory, so later questions about any of those facts can be answered.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Evaluations with Stated Reasons
payload.description: Use during extraction when a speaker explicitly praises or evaluates another person's role, abilities, or character and gives specific qualities or reasons for that evaluation.
content: When a speaker explicitly states a positive evaluation of someone (e.g., calling them a perfect mentor, great leader, etc.) and provides specific supporting qualities or reasons, create a durable memory candidate that captures the subject, the evaluation, and the exact stated reasons.
Do not merge these specific reasons only into a generic encouragement or support event; keep them as an explicit part of the evaluation so the reason remains answerable.
Stop after recording the evaluation and the stated reasons; do not infer additional qualities or reasons that were not mentioned.

candidates.solves: When a speaker gives an explicit positive evaluation of another person's role or character (e.g., calling them a perfect mentor) and states specific reasons or qualities, extraction often captures only the generic encouragement and drops the decisive attributes. This makes later questions about why the speaker holds that opinion unanswerable from memory.

payload.name: Extract Multiple Distinct Events from One Message
payload.description: When a message or conversational turn contains multiple explicitly stated events or facts about different people, use this during extraction so each event is captured.
content: During extraction, if a message contains multiple explicit events or facts about different people (or about the same person at different times), create a separate event candidate for each distinct event.
Do not let one salient event cause other explicitly mentioned events in the same message to be omitted; check the whole message and adjacent turns for additional stated facts.
Stop once every explicitly stated distinct event has its own candidate; do not infer events that were not stated.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes captures only one salient event from a message that explicitly contains several, causing other people's actions to be lost. This skill ensures each explicitly stated event is extracted as its own memory candidate.

payload.name: Extract nicknames from direct address
payload.description: During extraction, when a speaker directly addresses someone using a nickname or shortened name, create a relationship memory capturing that nickname.
content: During extraction, identify nicknames or shortened names used in direct address (e.g., 'Hey Jo', 'Thanks Mike'). Create a relationship memory recording that the speaker uses that nickname for the named person, even when the same message also contains an event or other state.
Do not merge the nickname only into an event candidate; make it a separate relationship memory so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only nicknames explicitly stated in direct address; do not infer or generalize beyond the exact term used.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes captures only the main event from a message and omits nicknames used in direct address (e.g., 'Hey Jo', 'Thanks Mike'). This causes later questions about what one person calls another to fail, because the nickname was never stored as a durable relationship memory.

payload.name: Preserve All Listed Items in Offer Enumerations
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message lists multiple services, offerings, or coordinated items a person provides; apply before finalizing a candidate.
content: During extraction, when a speaker enumerates two or more services, offerings, or components in a single statement (e.g., 'mentoring and training'), include every listed item in the memory candidate; do not drop one element when paraphrasing.
If a coordinated pair is expressed with 'and' or a list, treat each element as an explicit fact; a summary such as 'mentoring' for 'mentoring and training' loses information.
Stop after capturing all explicitly listed items; do not add services or components the speaker did not mention.

candidates.solves: Extraction from an offer or service description often drops one item when a message lists multiple coordinated services; the resulting memory is incomplete and cannot support later questions about what is offered.

payload.name: Extract Individual Attributes from Enumerated Group Lists
payload.description: When a user assigns distinct traits to each member of a group (e.g., pets, family) in one message, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a message assigns specific attributes to each member of an enumerated group (e.g., 'oldest is relaxed, second is playful...'), create a candidate for each member-attribute pair, not only a general summary.
Record the member identifier (e.g., oldest, youngest, named pet) and its stated attribute(s) in a durable memory (state or relationship), with the speaker as subject.
Keep the general affectionate or relational framing in a separate candidate if present, but do not let it substitute for the specific per-member facts.
Stop after one candidate per distinct member-attribute statement; do not infer attributes not explicitly stated.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes collapses a user's explicit enumeration of distinct traits for multiple group members into a single general sentiment memory, losing the individual facts needed to answer later questions. This Skill ensures each enumerated attribute pair is captured.

payload.name: Extract Factual Answers as State Memories
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about a pet, person, or possession with concrete factual details, create a state memory during extraction even without emotional or preference language.
content: During extraction, treat direct factual answers (e.g., what a pet eats, a person's role, an item's condition) as state memory candidates even when the message contains no preference or emotion words.
Attribute the fact to the specific subject named and preserve the exact details stated; do not wait for repetition or a like/dislike framing.
Stop after capturing the explicit facts in the answer; do not infer additional attributes.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes skips concrete factual statements about a user's pets, possessions, or people when the message is casual or directly answers a question, because no preference or emotional cue triggers candidate generation. This skill ensures explicit factual answers are captured as durable state memories.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Evaluative Words in Extracted Memories
payload.description: During extraction, when a memory candidate's source statement contains an explicit adjective or evaluative phrase describing a person, group, bond, event, or experience, preserve that exact wording in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if the speaker uses an explicit evaluative adjective or phrase (e.g., 'awesome', 'great', 'terrible', 'the best part'), include that exact wording in the memory content; do not replace it with a broader paraphrase like 'strong bonds' or 'positive experience'.
When a later message elaborates on the same statement, update the existing memory to add the explicit descriptor rather than creating a new candidate or leaving the paraphrase unchanged.
Keep the memory compact: capture the relationship or entity and the exact evaluative term(s) in one memory; do not enumerate synonyms or expand into unrelated details.
Apply only to explicit first-person descriptions; do not infer evaluative words that the speaker did not say.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction often paraphrases or generalizes a speaker's explicit evaluative description (e.g., 'our team bond is awesome') into an abstract summary, losing the exact wording that future questions may ask for.

payload.name: Extract Object Descriptions from Referenced-Item Exchanges
payload.description: Use during extraction when one speaker asks about or comments on an object the other speaker just showed or mentioned, and the reply identifies or describes that object.
content: During extraction, when a speaker refers to an object with a demonstrative or pronoun ('this map', 'that picture', 'it') and the other speaker replies by identifying or describing the object, resolve the referent from the prior turn and create a candidate memory for the object and its description.

If the exchange shows the object was shown or shared, record an event memory with the sharer, the recipient, and the object identity; otherwise record a state memory for the owner/object only if ownership is explicit.
Do not require the object name to be repeated in the reply; use the preceding question or comment as context to identify the object.
Emit at most one memory per such exchange unless the reply states additional distinct facts about a different subject.

candidates.solves: Conversations where an object is shown or mentioned and then identified only in a reply to a follow-up question are missed because the subject is expressed by a demonstrative or pronoun. This skill makes extraction resolve the referent across turns so showing/sharing events and object descriptions are stored.

payload.name: Capture Explicit Rationale with Stated Opinions
payload.description: When a speaker states an opinion, belief, or preference and explicitly provides a reason or purpose, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a speaker expresses an opinion, belief, or preference and explicitly states the reason or purpose (e.g., 'important to...', 'because...', 'so that...'), capture both the stance and the stated rationale in the same candidate.
Preserve the rationale verbatim enough to answer why-questions; do not reduce the candidate to only the stance.
Stop after capturing the stance and its explicitly stated rationale; do not infer unstated reasons or expand to other topics.

candidates.solves: This solves the problem of extraction candidates capturing only a speaker's stance or activity while dropping the explicitly stated reason or purpose, which later prevents answering why-questions about the speaker's beliefs.

payload.name: Preserve all explicitly listed experience elements
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message explicitly enumerates multiple distinct aspects that made an experience positive (e.g., relaxing, enjoyable, fun) and the memory should preserve each listed element.
content: During extraction, when a message explicitly lists multiple distinct elements of an experience (e.g., 'fresh air, peacefulness, and a cozy cabin made it a retreat'), preserve every stated element in the memory, including abstract qualities as well as concrete items.

Do not replace the enumeration with a single vague paraphrase or capture only the most concrete item; either create separate durable memories for each element or list all elements explicitly in one memory.
Stop after the explicitly stated elements are captured; do not infer additional aspects or expand into unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: When extraction collapses a message that explicitly lists multiple distinct reasons or elements that made an experience positive (enjoyable, relaxing, etc.) into a single vague paraphrase, it loses verifiable facts. This skill preserves each explicitly stated element so later evidence-based questions can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve All Explicit Preference Facets Before Duplicate Skip
payload.description: Use when a message states a preference or feeling with multiple explicit reasons or facets, or when a candidate is about to be SKIPped as a duplicate; preserve every explicit facet and only SKIP if the target memory already contains all of them.
content: During extraction, if a speaker gives multiple explicit reasons or facets for one preference, feeling, or state (e.g., emotional benefit plus practical benefit), include every explicitly stated facet in the candidate content; do not keep only the most prominent or emotional one.

During CRUD decisions, before SKIPping a candidate as 'duplicate information already represented', compare the candidate's explicit facts with the existing/updated memory. If the candidate contains any explicit facet not present in the target, do not SKIP it; create or update the memory to include that facet.
Capture only explicitly stated facets and stop; do not infer additional benefits or exhaustively expand the memory.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes loses explicit preference details when a candidate captures only one facet of a multi-faceted statement and is then skipped as a duplicate even though the omitted facet is not stored anywhere. This skill ensures all explicitly stated facets are extracted and that duplicate SKIP decisions happen only when the target memory truly contains every candidate fact.

payload.name: Attribute Relational Views to Speaking User
payload.description: During extraction in multi-party conversations, if one speaker explicitly states a view about someone or something, attribute the memory to that speaker, not to the conversation partner who agrees or responds.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly frames how they view someone or something (e.g., 'pets feel like family'), record the speaker as the subject of the memory, regardless of whether another participant expresses agreement or a similar view.
If two participants each state their own view, create separate memories for each speaker with their own subject; do not merge one speaker's statement into the other's existing memory.
Before attributing a relational statement to an existing memory, verify that the memory's subject matches the speaker of the message; if not, create a new memory for the correct speaker.
Stop after capturing each speaker's explicit view once per relationship; do not duplicate or expand with agreement phrases.

candidates.solves: Extraction in multi-party conversations sometimes attributes one speaker's explicit relational view to the other participant, causing facts to be stored under the wrong person. This skill ensures statements are attributed to the actual speaker, preventing cross-speaker contamination of relationship memories.

payload.name: Extract All Explicit Facts from a Message
payload.description: When a single message explicitly states multiple distinct durable facts (e.g., an event plus a peripheral detail), during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a message contains multiple distinct explicit facts (e.g., a speaker states they signed up for a class and also describes an incidental encounter), create a separate candidate for each distinct fact; do not let one salient detail suppress the other.
Identify the primary stated action, plan, or event and ensure it is captured, even if the message also contains a concrete or colorful peripheral detail.
Stop after all explicitly stated durable facts have been captured; do not add unstated inferences or duplicate candidates for the same fact.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a user message explicitly states multiple distinct durable facts, the extractor may capture only the most salient or concrete detail and omit the primary action or plan, leading to missing memories. This skill ensures all explicitly stated facts, especially the primary event or plan, are captured in separate candidates without inventing unstated details.

payload.name: Extract Every Distinct Explicit Fact
payload.description: When a single message contains multiple distinct explicit facts and one fact is more salient or is the main topic, use this during extraction and CRUD.
content: During extraction, if a message states two or more independent explicit facts, create one candidate memory for each fact rather than a single candidate centered on the most salient topic.
Do not skip an explicit durable fact because it is mentioned in passing, as background, or in the same message as a more prominent topic; if it is clearly stated, extract it as its own candidate.
During CRUD, when adding or merging candidates, preserve all explicitly stated distinct facts; accepting a salient candidate must not cause other explicit facts to be dropped or overwritten.
Stop after capturing each distinct fact; do not infer unmentioned details or expand into related topics.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes records only the most salient statement from a message and omits other explicitly stated durable facts, leaving memory incomplete for later questions. This skill ensures each distinct explicit fact in a message becomes its own candidate and is preserved through CRUD.

payload.name: Resolve Pronoun References to Prior Entities
payload.description: Use during extraction when a message states a fact using a pronoun (it, this, that, they) that refers to an entity mentioned earlier in the conversation.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a pronoun (it, this, that, they) that refers to an entity explicitly mentioned earlier in the conversation, resolve the referent from the recent context and create a candidate memory for the stated fact about that entity, even if the entity name is not repeated.

If the stated fact includes a relative time phrase such as 'a year ago' or 'last month', resolve it against the message/session timestamp to an absolute year/date and record that in the memory content (e.g., bought/started in YYYY).
Choose the closest semantically matching antecedent when multiple candidates exist; if no clear referent exists, do not invent one and stop after extracting the fact.

candidates.solves: The construction agent sometimes skips a factual statement because the message uses a pronoun instead of repeating the entity name, so facts about previously mentioned pets, people, or objects are never stored even though the referent is clear from the conversation context.

payload.name: Extract Explicitly Stated Personal Values
payload.description: When a user explicitly says something is important to them, matters to them, or that they value it (e.g., 'X is important to me', 'I value X', 'X matters to me'), during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a user explicitly states a personal value or importance, create a separate durable preference or state candidate preserving that value in the user's own words, even if it is given as the reason for an activity.
If multiple distinct values are stated in one message, capture each value explicitly rather than absorbing them only into an event/activity memory.
During CRUD, when merging such a value into an existing memory, retain the explicit importance wording; do not replace it with only a description of the related activity.
Stop after capturing the stated values; do not infer additional values not explicitly mentioned.

candidates.solves: Extraction candidates often paraphrase a user's explicit statement of personal importance into an activity description, dropping the value itself (e.g., keeping the activity but losing that something is important to the user). This skill ensures explicitly stated values and importance are preserved as durable preference/state memories, so later questions asking why the user does something can be answered.

payload.name: Preserve Resolved Dates When Updating Event Memories
payload.description: When updating or enriching an existing event memory with a candidate that includes a relative time phrase, resolve the phrase to an absolute date and store it in both content and world_start.
content: When applying an UPDATE or MERGE to an existing event memory using a candidate with a relative time phrase, resolve the phrase against the message/session timestamp and write the absolute date (e.g., 2023-04-24) into the memory content and world_start.
Do not copy vague wording such as 'the previous day' or 'recently' into the updated content; the stored memory must stand alone without the source message.
If the existing memory already has a world_start, overwrite it with the resolved date for the new event unless the new event is a separate occurrence.
Stop after updating the single affected memory; do not propagate the date to unrelated memories.

candidates.solves: During memory updates, agents sometimes copy relative time phrases like 'yesterday' into the stored content and fail to carry over the correctly resolved absolute date, causing the fact's date to become ambiguous or lost. This skill prevents that by requiring the resolved absolute date to replace relative wording and update world_start whenever enriching an existing event memory.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Event Timing in Extraction
payload.description: Use when a message states when an event, possession, or achievement happened using a relative or explicit time phrase, during extraction or memory update.
content: During extraction, if a message reports when an event, possession, or achievement occurred (e.g., 'a few years ago', 'last summer', 'in 2021'), include that time phrase explicitly in the candidate content.
Do not replace the stated time with the message/session date; keep the speaker's wording so future questions about timing can be answered.
Also apply when updating an existing memory that later gains an explicit time qualifier.
Stop at the stated time; do not compute or infer an exact date unless the speaker supplies one.

candidates.solves: Extraction sometimes keeps the descriptive or emotional details of an event or possession but drops explicit temporal qualifiers such as 'a few years ago', so later questions about when it happened cannot be answered. This skill ensures that explicit timing stated in the source is preserved in the extracted memory.

payload.name: Extract distinct facts alongside relative time expressions
payload.description: When a message contains a relative time expression plus other factual claims such as counts, attendance, or outcomes, extract each distinct fact as its own memory candidate during construction.
content: During extraction, treat each message as a bundle of distinct factual claims: numeric quantities, event details, stated preferences, and relative time expressions each belong in their own candidate.

When a message mixes a relative time expression with another fact (e.g., '7 people attended' and 'want to do it again next month'), resolve the time expression for the relevant candidate and still create a separate candidate for the other fact.
Do not let applying a time-resolution skill suppress extraction of the remaining substantive facts in the same message.
Stop after each distinct fact is captured once; do not add extra candidates for paraphrases or inferred details.

candidates.solves: Construction sometimes only resolves a relative time expression and fails to extract other explicit facts in the same message (e.g., attendance counts, outcomes). This skill ensures each distinct claim in a message becomes its own memory candidate.

payload.name: Preserve Cumulative Counts of Repeated Events
payload.description: When a message reports another occurrence in a series of discrete events for the same person (e.g., a second, fourth, or latest win/milestone), use this guidance.
content: During extraction, when a speaker reports a repeated discrete event with an ordinal or 'another' (e.g., second tournament win, another visit), include the ordinal/cumulative count in the candidate content; do not store only the latest occurrence.

During CRUD, before updating an existing memory with a new occurrence of the same event type for the same subject, search the pool for prior occurrences; preserve the earlier occurrence(s) instead of overwriting their content and date.
If prior occurrences exist, write a compact count memory or add the cumulative total to the updated memory so the number of occurrences is explicit (e.g., 'has now won N tournaments').
Stop once the cumulative count is recorded; do not enumerate every occurrence or aggregate different event types.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes UPDATE an existing event memory with a newer occurrence of the same kind, overwriting earlier facts and losing the ability to answer count questions. This skill ensures repeated discrete events are preserved and their cumulative count is made explicit.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Time in Extracted Memories
payload.description: When extracting or updating an event/state memory from a statement containing a relative time expression (e.g., 'last month', 'last Friday', 'next month'), resolve it from the message timestamp and record the absolute date.
content: During extraction, if a statement contains a relative time expression (e.g., 'last month', 'last Friday', 'next month'), resolve it to an absolute calendar date or month using the message/session timestamp.

Include the resolved absolute time explicitly in the memory content (e.g., 'lost his job in October 2023'), not just a relative phrase like 'last month'; align world_start/world_end with the resolved date.
When updating an existing memory, preserve the same absolute anchor and add the newly resolved timing if missing.
Stop after anchoring the stated time; do not infer further dates or expand the memory with additional unstated details.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes stores relative time expressions verbatim without anchoring them to the message timestamp, so later questions about when an event happened cannot be answered from the memory. This skill ensures relative time references in extracted event/state memories are resolved to absolute dates and recorded explicitly.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Time in Event Extraction
payload.description: When extracting an event memory from a message that contains a relative time expression such as 'last summer', 'yesterday', or 'two weeks ago', resolve it to an absolute date from the message timestamp instead of using the message date.
content: During extraction, when a message describes an event with a relative time expression (e.g., 'last summer', 'yesterday', 'two weeks ago'), resolve it to an absolute date using the message/session timestamp and set the event memory's world_start (and world_end if bounded) to that resolved date, not the message date.
Include the resolved time in the candidate content (e.g., 'in summer 2022') so the timing remains searchable; do not leave only vague phrasing such as 'during her vacation'.
Stop after capturing the event and its resolved timing; do not expand into additional memories unless the message contains other distinct facts.

candidates.solves: Extraction often drops relative time references in event statements and defaults event dates to the message timestamp, so later questions about when something happened cannot be answered. This skill makes extractors resolve relative temporal expressions to absolute dates and store them with the event memory.

payload.name: Resolve Relative Event Start Dates
payload.description: During extraction, when a message describes an event or state start with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last week', 'recently'), apply this guidance to set the correct world_start.
content: When a message describes an event or state start with a relative time phrase (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last month', 'recently'), resolve the start date from the message/session timestamp by subtracting the indicated duration; never use the message date as the event start unless the phrase explicitly says 'today' or 'now'.
For vague phrases like 'a few days ago', record an approximate earlier date in world_start and preserve the original relative wording in memory content so the uncertainty remains traceable.
Keep this resolution consistent across extraction and any later ADD/UPDATE/MERGE; do not drop the relative expression in favor of an overly precise date.

candidates.solves: When extracting the start date of an event or state from a message that uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'a few days ago', 'last week'), the agent incorrectly sets the event's world_start to the message timestamp, losing the temporal offset. This skill teaches the agent to resolve the relative expression against the message/session timestamp and preserve the nuance.

payload.name: Extract Past Event Times from Relative Phrases
payload.description: When a message states an event happened a relative time ago (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week', 'two days ago'), extract it with an absolute date.
content: During extraction, when a message contains a relative past-time phrase (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last month', 'last week', 'two days ago') attached to an event, purchase, action, or change in state, create an event or state candidate for that fact and resolve the phrase to an approximate absolute date/time using the message/session timestamp.
Include the resolved absolute time (e.g., 'bought X in January 2022') in the memory content or world_start rather than storing only the relative phrase.
If the exact day is unknown, record the best known precision (year, month, or date) and do not infer extra details beyond the stated event; stop after capturing the event and its time.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip statements that describe when a past event occurred using relative time phrases (e.g., 'a year ago', 'last week'), leaving no memory for future temporal queries. This skill ensures such relative past times are resolved to absolute dates and stored with the event.

payload.name: Preserve Explicit Search and Attempt Details
payload.description: Use when a message describes searching for, losing, or failing to find an object or attempting something without success; preserve the specific object, duration, and unsuccessful outcome in the memory.
content: During extraction, when a speaker describes searching for or losing something (e.g., 'searching for my keys for the last half hour with no luck'), create an event/state memory that includes the exact object, the stated duration or timeframe, and the unsuccessful outcome (e.g., 'could not find').

Also include any explicitly stated recurrence (e.g., 'losing it every week') as a separate facet, but do not replace the concrete search details with only the emotional reaction or a summary like 'lost his keys.'
Stop after preserving the explicitly stated search facts; do not infer reasons, locations, or outcomes beyond what was said.

candidates.solves: During memory extraction, the agent often summarizes an explicit problem or struggle (e.g., losing an item, searching without success) into a generic emotional or event statement, dropping concrete details such as the object involved, the duration, and the unsuccessful outcome. Future questions ask about those dropped details. This skill addresses preserving explicit facts about searches and failed attempts in extraction.

payload.name: Preserve Explicitly Stated Problems and Difficulties
payload.description: When a user explicitly describes a task, search, or situation as tough, difficult, annoying, or a problem, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when the speaker explicitly labels an ongoing goal, search, or task as difficult, tough, annoying, or a problem, preserve that evaluation in the memory content instead of summarizing only the goal or preference.
Record the subject, the challenged goal, and the stated difficulty (e.g., 'finding a pet-friendly place has been tough' becomes a memory that the person had difficulty finding pet-friendly housing).
Keep the difficulty in the same candidate as the related goal or activity; do not create an extra memory solely for the emotion.
Stop after the difficulty and its object are captured; do not infer or add other unstated problems.

candidates.solves: Extraction often records a user's stated goal, preference, or ongoing activity but drops explicit evaluations that the goal is hard, tough, annoying, or a problem. Future questions asking what problems the user faced then cannot be answered from memory. This skill preserves those explicitly stated difficulties across any domain.

payload.name: Extract Expressed Aesthetic Preferences
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly says they find a place, scene, or sensory aspect beautiful, gorgeous, or otherwise appealing, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly expresses admiration or preference for a visual or sensory aspect of a place, experience, or object (e.g., 'the colors are so beautiful', 'the view is amazing'), create a durable preference memory recording the speaker as subject and the appreciated aspect as object.

Capture the aspect in the speaker's own words and resolve relative time from the message timestamp; do not require a standalone opinion sentence - the statement may occur within a suggestion, plan, or small talk.
Stop after the stated aspect; do not infer additional likes or extend the same admiration to unmentioned features.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip explicit statements of admiration or preference when they appear inside suggestions, plans, or small talk, leaving no memory to answer later questions about what a person likes or finds beautiful.

payload.name: Capture Specifically Missed Aspects
payload.description: When a speaker expresses missing, longing, or nostalgia for a past experience or activity, during extraction.
content: During extraction, when a speaker uses miss, misses, missing, nostalgic, or longs for about a past experience, capture the exact object of that feeling, not just the broader activity.
Preserve any explicit qualifiers or descriptive phrases attached to the missed object (e.g., 'peaceful moments out in nature') so the memory answers what specifically was missed.
If the statement names both a general activity and a specific missed aspect, record both with the specific aspect as the primary object of the miss.
Stop after capturing the stated missed object and its qualifiers; do not add inferred reasons or unrelated details.

candidates.solves: Extraction often records the general activity when someone says they miss an experience, dropping the precise aspect they miss (e.g., 'the peaceful moments'). This skill ensures future memories retain the exact object and qualifiers of missing/nostalgia statements so downstream questions can be answered.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Missing or Longing Statements
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly says they miss, long for, or feel the absence of something, during extraction.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states they miss, long for, or feel the absence of something (e.g., 'I miss...', 'really missing...', 'can't do that here...'), create a separate durable state or preference memory capturing what is missed and the reason if stated.
Do not merge the missing/longing into a positive appreciation memory; keep it as its own candidate so future questions about what the speaker lacks or misses can be answered.
Capture the speaker's own words for what is missed and any explicitly stated contrast (e.g., city vs. nature); stop after one memory per distinct missed subject.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction omits explicit statements of missing or longing for something, capturing only the positive appreciation (e.g., value, enjoyment) and losing the key absence fact, so future questions about what the speaker lacks or misses cannot be answered from memory.
